title: synthetic-tokenflow-prober-ws-sse: high-fidelity load harness for streaming chat
creator: Maya Chen
description: Create a reusable, configurable load harness that simulates realistic streaming chat traffic over both SSE and WebSocket protocols. The harness ("synthetic-tokenflow-prober") will focus on token-level throughput (tokens/sec), client-side p95 end-to-end latency, connection churn and reconnection patterns, and regression detection across nightly runs. It must support variable sequence length distributions, conversation turn-taking, prefix KV caching behavior, and optional server-side simulated throttling/fallbacks to evaluate graceful degradation.
goals: Produce reproducible tokens/sec benchmarks for chat/completion routes across model families and quantization profiles
Track p95 end-to-end response latency per-session and per-token with 99th-percentile tails for regression detection
Surface regressions automatically (diff against baseline) and open alerts when p95 or token throughput deviates beyond configurable thresholds
Be protocol-agnostic: identical workload semantics for SSE and WS, plus multiplexed client simulation
Integrate results with Prometheus/Grafana and store canonical artifacts for audit and postmortem
approach_summary: Build the driver in Go (reuse existing low-level connection libraries) to maximize concurrency and low CPU overhead. Workload model defined as a YAML scenario: client cohorts, turn distributions, token-length histograms, inter-token delays (stream pacing), and network continuity profiles (packet loss/reconnect). The driver emits metric series (tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency, connection failures, reconnect rate) to Prometheus and writes canonical CSV/JSON artifacts to the benchmarks bucket. Regression detection uses nightly baseline comparisons with a configurable alert window and a small statistical test (Welch's t-test over p95 samples) + heuristic change thresholds.
implementation_notes: Client behavior: support both server-sent events (SSE) and WebSocket streaming; implement identical tokenizer and simulated server payloads to keep client-side parsing impact consistent
Sequence distribution: use realistic histograms derived from production sampling (convo_lengths_v2) — configurable per cohort
KV cache emulation: driver should optionally warm KV cache between turns and measure cache-hit vs cold-run latency
Backpressure and throttling: harness can inject 429/503 responses to simulate degraded upstream and verify fallback routing
Observability: emit prometheus metrics + structured per-session logs with session_id, seed, scenario_name, final_token_count
Resource footprint: run multiple driver instances across multiple machines for scale; provide a lightweight client binary for k8s Job execution
Determinism: seedable random generator and scenario dump to reproduce failing runs
acceptance_criteria: Driver can run identical YAML scenario in SSE and WS modes and produce matching workload semantics
Metrics exported to Prometheus and dashboard shows tokens/sec and p95 latency per-model and per-cohort
Nightly regression pipeline compares current run to baseline and posts results to #benchmarks with pass/fail and attached artifact links
A minimal regression: 15% p95 increase or 20% throughput drop triggers an alert and creates an issue template populated with the failing artifacts
Documentation: runbook and example scenarios committed to repo and a Confluence page describing knobs and how to interpret dashboards
risks_and_mitigations: False positives from noisy samples: mitigate by requiring both statistical test and absolute threshold before alerting
Client skew vs production: mitigate by sampling production conv lengths and including a 'production-approx' cohort
Driver-induced bottleneck: measure driver CPU/NET and provide scale-out guidance; recommend Go runtime settings
Data sensitivity: no PII should be included in scenarios; use synthetic prompt sets and tokenizers
